title: External or gradational forces and resultant landforms
competency: Describe weathering, erosion and the landforms they make.

keywords.def: A force acting on the earth's surface from outside that levels its ups and downs.
The lowering of the land by wearing away of the surface. It consists of weathering and erosion.
The breaking down of rocks into smaller particles.
Rock layers peeling off because of day and night temperature changes (onion-skin weathering).
The movement of broken rock and soil from one place to another by running water, wind, ice or waves.

en.text: External forces act on the surface from outside and level its ups and downs, by denudation and deposition. Denudation is weathering plus erosion. Physical weathering breaks rocks into pieces (temperature change, frost, plants and animals); chemical weathering changes the rock inside, like rain dissolving limestone into caves.

screens.title: Peeling rock
screens.ask: A large rock in the hot Danakil is very hot by day and cold at night. After many years its outer layers peel off. Why?
opts: It expands by day and shrinks by night
screens.after: The rock expands in the heat and contracts in the cold, again and again, until layers peel off. This is exfoliation.

screens.title: External forces
paras: External forces act upon the earth's surface from the outside.
They level the ups and downs, in two ways: denudation and deposition.
Denudation is the lowering of the land by wearing away the surface. It consists of weathering and erosion.
Weathering is the breaking down of rocks into smaller particles.

screens.title: Two kinds of weathering
paras: Physical weathering breaks rocks into smaller pieces.
Chemical weathering completely changes the inside structure of rocks.
table: Rain action: carbonic acid dissolves limestone into caves
Frost action: ice in cracks splits rock; pieces pile up as screes
Plants and animals: bacteria and organic acids break down minerals
screens.note: Caves have stalactites (hanging down), stalagmites (growing up) and pillars (where the two join).

en.text: Erosion moves broken rock and soil by running water, wind, moving ice or sea waves. Running water causes sheet, rill and gully erosion. Wind is strongest in deserts and forms sand dunes, barchans and loess deposits.

screens.title: A ditch after rain
screens.ask: After heavy kiremt rain, a deep wide ditch appears on a bare hillside. What made it?
screens.after: Floods of running water cut deep, wide channels called gullies.

screens.title: Erosion
paras: Erosion is the movement of broken rock and soil particles from one place to another.
It is done by running water, wind, moving ice or sea waves.
Rivers erode, transport and deposit material.
table: Surface water moves in a wide flow

screens.title: Wind erosion
paras: Wind is the strongest force of erosion in deserts.
A sand dune is a small hill of sand made by the wind.
A barchan is a crescent-moon-shaped sand hill.
A loess deposit is fertile soil laid down by wind.
